title: Tiled NVTX + Nsight trace: prefetch-window and kernel launch jitter investigation
body:
Summary:

This note captures the investigation run May 2026 into a recurrent drop in GPU occupancy and bursty tail latency observed on long-context (1k-4k) decoder workloads. The failure mode shows as episodic 10-40% SM occupancy drops lasting ~40-140ms and coincident CPU-side spikes in kernel launch time. Goal was to reconstruct timelines across many traces, isolate the small-window phenomenon we call the "prefetch window", and propose mitigations and a short runbook.

Why this is different:
- Rather than a single monolithic Nsight capture, we "tile" long traces into 100ms NVTX-aligned segments and aggregate kernel-start histograms across requests. This makes small recurring gaps visible that get washed out in full-session overviews.
- We correlate device-side pci/copy events with host launch latencies and cudaGraph capture/execute boundaries to show an interaction between async host staging and launch batching.

Observations (empirical):
- Pattern: at ~every Nth token (varies by microbatch and sequence length), there is a 60-140us stall where no kernels are executing on the GPU, followed by 0.8–2.5ms jitter in subsequent kernel start times. Aggregated occupancy shows a ~22% relative drop for L=2048 experiments (microbatch 4) during these windows.
- NVTX-tiling revealed that stalls align with a short period of heavy async memcpy activity (H2D) on stream 2 while compute is on stream 0; but H2D bursts do not fully explain the timing — we also see increased host-side enqueue latency measured by our XLA wrapper (~200–600us).
- CUDA Graphs: in runs where we enable cudaGraph capture per-request, the capture window boundaries introduce a serialization point. When capture ends and graph launch begins, we observe kernel launch consolidation on the host causing a brief serialization spike.
- KV cache reuse: requests that hit the KV cache heavily (prefix reuse) show lower incidence, suggesting that the prefetch-window is exacerbated by fresh key/value population work and accompanying small kernels that are launch-heavy.

Method: how we gathered data
1) Modified nvtx tagging in runtime to emit a "tile-id" every 100ms (host clock) plus token-level tags.
2) Collected 120 captures from a 8-GPU p4d-like cluster node (test harness), each capture limited to ~1.6s total and saved as .ncu files.
3) Sliced each capture into 100ms tiles and exported per-tile kernel start times and durations using ncu CLI JSON export.
4) Built aggregate histograms of kernel inter-arrival times and kernel density maps across tile positions.
5) Cross-referenced host-side traces (clock-sync'd) to measure cudaLaunch and memcpy enqueue latencies and to mark cudaGraph capture/launch boundaries.

Key commands / scripts used (for reproducibility):
- nvtx tagging: runtime patch at git:serving-runtime:tools/nvtx_tiler.rb (attached doc page)
- capture: ncu --target-processes all --capture-range timeline --replay-mode application --output ./trace_$RUN.ncu ./bin/latency_test --config run.yaml
- export: ncu --import ./trace_$RUN.ncu --export ./trace_$RUN.json --section "Scheduler" --section "Memory"
- tile-slice: python tools/tiler/slice_tiles.py --input trace_$RUN.json --tile-ms 100 --out tiles/$RUN/

Findings (detailed):
- Host enqueue jitter: our host-side instrumentation shows cudaLaunch API calls cluster tightly but with intermittent outliers. The outliers coincide with small memcpy descriptors being submitted near the same time (driver work queue contention). The driver appears to serialize some submissions when a mix of copy and kernel workloads are enqueued to different streams on the same host thread.
- Small kernel flood: sequences that populate KV caches run many small kernels (<40us). When many such kernels are in-flight (microbatch 4–8), we see host-side batching of launches which reduces parallelism and leaves SMs idle while the driver commits the launches.
- CUDA Graph capture boundaries: repeated capture/instantiate/launch cycles show an internal driver path that synchronizes on graph instantiation for short periods; if capture windows align with prefetch phases, the handoff causes a hole.
- L2/backpressure interaction: tiles show occasional L2-bandwidth bursts immediately before stalls. Hypothesis: bursts of H2D saturate the DMA engines, driver reorders submissions, and small-kernel launches get delayed waiting for DMA completion due to prioritization or internal sequencing.

Quantitative snippets (representative):
- L=2048, microbatch=4: mean occupancy outside windows 83% -> inside window 64% (relative -22.9%).
- Tail latency 95th percentile increase during episodes: +18% for that workload config.
- Kernel inter-arrival median outside windows 40us, inside windows 1.2ms (x30).

Hypotheses and tests run:
- H1: driver serialization between copy and kernel submissions causes the host-side enqueue jitter. Test: stagger copy submissions by 50us using a small host-side sleep. Result: measured reduction in outliers, occupancy stalls reduced by ~65% in synthetic replay.
- H2: too-fine-grained cudaGraph capture/launch oscillations cause serialization. Test: expand capture windows to encompass the full decode loop. Result: reduces the number of capture/launch boundaries and reduces stall frequency by ~75% on our bench but at cost of higher memory for graph instantiation (OOM risk for very long sequences).
- H3: stream priority mismatch. Test: move prefetch copies to a lower priority stream and compute to high priority. Result: small improvement; does not eliminate stalls, suggests driver-level ordering still influential.

Actionable mitigations (short list):
1) Batching small prefetch kernels: fuse tiny prefetch kernels into a single kernel when possible (backend change, medium effort).
2) Stagger async copy submission from host when many small copies are queued (cheap, host-side change). Put a 20–60us randomized jitter when queue size > threshold.
3) Adjust cudaGraph strategy: use per-sequence capture where memory allows; or capture a larger chunk that includes prefetch and initial decode to avoid boundary handoffs. Add guard for memory footprint.
4) Stream priorities: keep compute in the highest priority stream and prefer copy streams with lower priority. Verify behavior across driver versions.
5) Instrumentation: keep tiled NVTX traces in nightly perf runs; add automatic detection of occupancy-drop tiles and generate a regression alert.

Short runbook (for oncall):
- If you see repeated 95th-tail spikes on long-context tests:
  1) Pull last 24h tiled-nsight aggregate (tools/tiler/agg_report.py) and look for >15% occupancy-drop tiles at token positions.
  2) Check host enqueue histogram (tools/tiler/host_launch_hist.png) for outliers around the same tiles.
  3) If pattern present, enable "stagger-prefetch" toggle on the node config and re-run 3 synthetic traces.
  4) If that reduces stalls, schedule medium-effort change to KV prefetch kernel fusion; otherwise try expanded cudaGraph capture for the failing model.

Open questions / next work:
- Driver tuning: engage infra team to try different NVIDIA driver minor versions and observe whether serialization path changes. Early experiments show v525 -> v535 changes in enqueue behavior. Need more systematic tests.
- DMA and NVLink: further examine multi-GPU node traces (we ran single-GPU for this note). NVLink traffic during prefetch may produce different scheduling dynamics.
- Automated mitigation: implement adaptive capture window sizing (larger captures when many small kernels detected).

Appendix: links and artifacts
- scripts: tools/tiler/slice_tiles.py, tools/tiler/agg_report.py, runtime/patches/nvtx_tiler.rb (linked above PR).
- example low-noise reproduce: configs/repro/prefetch-window/repro_small_kernels.yaml
- short profiling checklist for future captures: 1) sync clocks across host & device, 2) ensure NVTX tiles present, 3) include host-side "enqueue" spans, 4) capture both memory and scheduler sections in NCU export.

Notes to self / TODO (informal):
- Move tiler into perf infra (cron job) and add Slack alert for occupancy-drop tiles.
- Re-run on p3/rtx-class machines to confirm cross-arch behavior.
- Review whether microbatch=1 has different pattern — initial runs show microbatch 1 still has holes but less frequent.

If useful I can extract the tiler aggregation notebook and attach a small interactive visualization next iteration.

-- Michael
